description: Babylon Station is a DMU Dubai team working at the intersection of cybersecurity, networking, and space health. We are building a secure health monitoring platform for astronauts on long-duration missions: it tracks vital signs, flags emerging health risks, detects tampered or faulty sensor data, and stays operational across delayed Earth–Mars communication links. Our mission is simple: when lives depend on data, that data must be trusted.
summary: Babylon Vitals is an on-board health monitoring prototype that helps an astronaut notice early that something is changing, without waiting for ground support. On a Mars mission, a message to Earth can take 3 to 22 minutes one way, so the crew member must be able to understand their own health first. The tool learns each astronaut's personal baseline over the first five days of a mission, then tracks six simple measures: heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, sleep and mood. Standard ranges can look fine while a person is quietly drifting away from their own normal. When several measures drift together, Babylon Vitals raises a clear multi-parameter warning, explains what changed in plain language, and prepares a short report for the flight surgeon. It also includes a scenario simulator and an Earth-link simulation that shows the communication delay. All data in the prototype is simulated.
details:
THE PROBLEM

Health monitoring on current missions relies heavily on ground teams who receive crew data and support the crew. On a mission to Mars, communication is delayed by roughly 3 to 22 minutes in each direction depending on planet positions. The crew will have to notice and act on early changes themselves. Checking readings only against standard population ranges can miss an early problem, because a reading can be "normal" for the population and still be abnormal for that one person.

WHAT WE BUILT

Babylon Vitals is a single-page web prototype that works offline. It shows one crew member's six health measures over a 14-day simulated mission:

- Live telemetry view (simulated feed) and a clickable body map that shows which system is affected.

- A personal baseline built from days 1 to 5 of the mission.

- Three clear states: Nominal, Caution and Warning.

- A multi-parameter warning that triggers when three or more measures drift from the personal baseline at the same time, even if every reading is still inside the standard range. A toggle switches between "standard ranges" and "own baseline" on the same data.

- A plain-language explanation of what changed, possible contributors (not a diagnosis), recommended next steps, and a ready-to-send report for the flight surgeon.

- A Mission What-If simulator (sleep deprivation, dehydration, high workload) and an Earth communication link simulation that shows the Earth-Mars delay and an on-board checklist while the crew waits for the reply.

- A manual entry option for measures such as mood.

HOW THE DETECTION WORKS

For each measure we compute the mean and standard deviation of the first five days (with a minimum spread to avoid false alarms). A reading more than 1.5 standard deviations from the personal baseline is a Caution; more than 2.5 is a Warning. A pattern warning is raised when at least three of the six measures are flagged. In our simulated scenario, the first drift appears on day 8 (heart rate) and the pattern warning on day 9, while all values remain inside standard ranges through day 14.

WHY IT MATTERS

Comparing each astronaut to their own baseline is supported by published space-medicine research. Our contribution is a simple, astronaut-facing tool that works when ground support is delayed and explains itself in plain language. In the public sources we reviewed we did not find a tool of this exact form, but we do not claim that none exists.

LIMITS AND FUTURE WORK

This is a prototype, not a medical device and not medical advice. The data is simulated and thresholds are example values that need clinical validation. Next steps: real wearable data input, clinical validation, per-person tuning, and secure handling of crew health data.

TOOLS

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript (single-page web app, works offline). Code written with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic) AI, then reviewed, tested and directed by the team. All data is simulated.
